chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl bin Ziyad, from Ahmad bin Muhammad bin Abu Nasr, from Hammad bin Isa, from Is'haq bin Ammar, who said:

I said to Abu Ibrahim (peace be upon him), 'A man buys a maid-servant, keeps her with him so that her value increases, and he intends to sell her. Is there Zakat upon her price?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'No, until he sells her.' I said, 'So when he sells her, should he purify (pay Zakat) on her price?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'No, until the year passes over it, and it (the price) is still in his hands.'

key_terms.يَحُولَ عَلَيْهِ الْحَوْل: The passing of a lunar year

ai.seo_question: When is Zakat due on a slave-servant or goods bought for resale?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Kafi clarifies the timing of Zakat on trade goods (al-‘urūḍ al-tijāriyyah) held for speculation, establishing that the liability attaches to the monetary value rather than the item itself. It specifies that the lunar year (ḥawl) for Zakat begins only after the sale is completed and the proceeds are in the owner's possession, a key distinction in Shia fiqh regarding the conversion of inventory to cash. This ruling underscores the principle that Zakat on trade goods is assessed on the realized wealth, not the potential value of the stock while it remains unsold.
